other_side: Zitron works from the same evidence and inverts all of it. He reads the AT&T migration not as a smarter stack but as the first move in cutting AI spend altogether — enterprises will save money "first by moving to open source models, then not using them at all", because in his view even open weights are expensive and of questionable use; he notes AT&T's headline 80-90% savings apply only to unspecified "certain applications" out of more than a thousand internal uses. He argues the whole debate about which model is cheapest misses the mechanism: "the problem is the amount of tokens that get burned", and labs are incentivised to build models that burn more of them. NVIDIA's Poolside deal, which the Brief reads as buying into the open-model future, he reads as vendor financing — NVIDIA "effectively becoming the GE Capital of AI", propping up customers who would otherwise fail. His sharpest structural point is one the Brief never addresses: "distillation requires a model to distill from", so a cheap open tier cannot outlive the frontier training spend it is supposedly replacing.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether the cheap end of the model market is a durable architecture or a symptom of a subsidy. Both accept the same facts: frontier capability has bunched up, most work does not need the top model, enterprises are actively moving volume to open weights, and open inference is not free because a token costs compute whoever produced it. The empirical question that will resolve is what happens to that open tier when frontier training slows — the observable is whether new open-weight models keep matching last-generation frontier quality once labs cut training budgets, and whether routed enterprise workloads grow or get switched off entirely at renewal. The residue is pure worldview: Whittemore sees firms discovering efficiency; Zitron sees firms beginning to leave. Whittemore is vindicated if routed open-model stacks become standard IT and total useful workload keeps rising as prices fall; Zitron if the migration turns out to be the penultimate step before abandonment and the open tier degrades without frontier models to distil from. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: neither disputes that most people do not need the frontier, and neither thinks open inference is actually cheap. Watch whether the next generation of open weights arrives on schedule, and at what quality.
